questions.stem: Roughly how many volts of static can destroy a computer chip, versus how many you must reach before you even feel a shock?

choices.text: A chip can be destroyed by as little as 100 volts, but you don't feel a shock until about 3,500 volts
A chip needs 3,500 volts to fail, and you feel shocks at 100 volts
Both thresholds are exactly 1,000 volts
Chips are immune to static below 10,000 volts

questions.explanation: A chip can be destroyed by as little as 100 volts, but humans don't feel a static shock until around 3,500 volts - so you can fry a board without feeling a thing.
questions.trap: The numbers are not reversed: the damage threshold (100 V) is far below the human-perception threshold (3,500 V).

questions.stem: What does an ESD strap do to protect components?

choices.text: It grounds the building's electrical system
It connects your wrist to the metal chassis, keeping you at the same electrical potential as the device
It adds extra voltage to the motherboard
It replaces the need to unplug the power

questions.explanation: An ESD strap connects your wrist to the metal chassis so you and the device stay at the same electrical potential, preventing a discharge.
questions.trap: You connect to the chassis, NOT to the building's ground - tying yourself to building ground is explicitly dangerous.

questions.stem: When storing loose components, which item shields them against static discharge?

choices.text: A clear plastic zipper bag
A paper envelope
Silver anti-static bags
A cardboard box

questions.explanation: Use anti-static bags - specifically the silver ones - to shield stored parts against discharge.
questions.trap: Ordinary clear plastic bags can actually generate static; the shielding silver anti-static bag is what's required.

questions.stem: What is the number-one rule of electrical safety before opening any device?

choices.text: Put on safety goggles
Bundle the cables with zip ties
Lift with your legs
Disconnect the power source first

questions.explanation: The number-one electrical-safety rule is to disconnect the power source before opening anything.
questions.trap: Goggles, cable management, and proper lifting are all good practices, but cutting power comes first.

questions.stem: Why is a power supply or laser-printer power unit dangerous even after being unplugged?

choices.text: Capacitors inside can store residual electricity and shock you
It will automatically reboot the computer
It releases toxic gas when opened
It magnetizes nearby drives

questions.explanation: Capacitors act like a sponge that still holds water after the faucet is off - they store residual power and can shock you. Don't open high-voltage units; replace the whole unit.
questions.trap: The danger is stored charge in capacitors, not a reboot or toxic gas.

questions.stem: A technician finds a high-voltage component like a power supply is faulty. What is the correct action?

choices.text: Open it and replace the internal capacitor
Do not open it; replace the whole unit
Discharge it by touching it with a screwdriver
Connect yourself to building ground, then open it

questions.explanation: Never open high-voltage components like a power supply. Replace the entire unit instead.
questions.trap: Connecting yourself to building ground is dangerous, and opening a power supply exposes you to stored charge - replace, don't repair.

questions.stem: When lifting a heavy server, what is the recommended technique?

choices.text: Bend at the waist and lift with your back
Lift quickly to get it over with
Lift with your legs to protect your back
Always lift alone to avoid coordination issues

questions.explanation: Protect your back by lifting with your legs, not your back.
questions.trap: Bending at the waist and lifting with the back is exactly the unsafe technique that causes injuries.

questions.stem: Messy cables on the floor present which hazard, and how should you address it?

choices.text: A fire hazard; soak them in water
An ESD hazard; ground each cable
A magnetic hazard; shield them with foil
A trip hazard; bundle them with Velcro or zip ties

questions.explanation: Loose cables are a major trip hazard; use Velcro straps or zip ties to bundle and manage them.
questions.trap: The risk here is tripping, not static or magnetism - and you never soak cables in water.

questions.stem: What fire-suppression agents do data centers use for electrical fires, and what must they avoid?

choices.text: Dry chemicals like FM-200 or CO2; never water
Water sprinklers; never chemicals
Sand buckets; never CO2
Foam only; never dry chemicals

questions.explanation: Data centers suppress fires with dry chemicals like FM-200 or carbon dioxide - never water, because electronics and water don't mix.
questions.trap: Water sprinklers would destroy the equipment and worsen an electrical fire; dry agents are required.

questions.stem: A device catches fire at a workstation. What is your first move?

choices.text: Throw water on it
Open the case to inspect the damage
Cut the power
Unplug nearby monitors first

questions.explanation: If a device catches fire, your first move is to cut the power.
questions.trap: Water on an electrical fire is dangerous; the priority is removing the power source, not inspecting or rearranging gear.
